entry.title: PlainSpeak: Understand everyday paperwork with local AI.
entry.summary: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady. PlainSpeak helps people understand everyday paperwork without rereading dense paragraphs. You can paste text, open a plain text file, or try the fictional appointment-letter sample. The app uses AI to explain the document in simpler language and point out details such as dates, locations, and actions. https://youtu.be/7FTC_TPzTn8 The video shows the setup guide, a fictional appointment notice, and the explanation produced by PlainSpeak. PlainSpeak on GitHub PlainSpeak is a browser app that uses the open-weight Gemma 3:1B model through Ollama running locally. The user provides a notice, and the app displays the model’s plain-language explanation alongside the original text. Running Gemma locally gives users more control over how the tool works. In the local Ollama setup, the document is processed on the user’s computer instead of being sent to a hosted AI model API. The project’s code is available for people to inspect and adapt. Instead of repeatedly searching a long notice for the important details, a user can start with a short explanation and check it against the original. PlainSpeak aims to make routine paperwork easier to get through. Best Use of Gemma

entry.title: Your AI assistant cited a law that does not exist. Here is the fix.
entry.summary: I watched an LLM cite a law that does not exist. Not a hypothetical: it produced 18 U.S.C. § 301 as the basis for a data-protection claim, and quoted Consumer Credit Act 1974 s. 157 for a rule that lives somewhere else entirely. Both looked authoritative. Both were wrong in ways only a lawyer — or a very suspicious engineer — would catch. Prompting did not fix it. "Be careful" is not a data structure. So we turned the rule into one. entry.title: The agent wrapped everything in try/catch and your errors disappeared
entry.summary: A payment method fails, and the UI shows a generic default instead of surfacing a failure. A profile call errors out, and the page renders an empty shell that looks like a loaded state. The ticket says it works in the demo, the build is green, and the real exception never reaches the caller's error path. The common cause is a blanket try/catch the agent added to "handle errors gracefully," with a default value returned where an error should have been propagated. The agent wraps the whole function body, catches everything, and returns a plausible object: an empty profile, an empty list, a zeroed record. Downstream code checks for a truthy value, the default object passes that check, and the caller cannot tell "missing" from "loaded." The upstream error is logged at warning level, if it is l…
